title: Carry Lab
context: Grade 4, the middle of the addition chapter and the half of column addition that actually goes wrong. An adult sees the same sums as the topic before with different digits. What the page is doing is asking for a trade: ten of one place for one of the next, stated four times in words before a single sum is worked. The carry is a quantity that moved, not a mark, and a child who writes it in the margin and adds it on at the end has learnt the mark.

writeup.why: Find out what happens when a column holds more than nine, and where the part that will not fit has to go.
writeup.look: A column mat with a small circle drawn above every column, a tray of tokens beside it, and a tally of the trades along the top.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Carry Lab' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns that had to trade against the columns closed so far, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one each time a circle fills and never once falling back. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The mat sits across the top of the working area, 800 by 400 at 207,202: a circle band 60 tall along its top holding one empty circle 48 across centred over every column, then headings 40 tall, then three addend rows of cells 64 tall, then a rule 6 tall across the full width, then the sum row 64 tall beneath it; the columns are 120 wide and the third addend row is ruled only when the third strip is on the mat. The token tray runs along the foot, 1086 by 120 at 64,610, and holds four kinds of token, each with its number printed on its face so it can be read as well as counted: a one is a square 28 by 28, a ten is a strip of ten of those squares standing on end at 28 by 56, a hundred is a block ruled ten by ten at 56 by 56, and a thousand is that same block drawn as a cube. Filling a column stands its tokens in the column from the floor upwards, exactly as many as its digits call for, never overlapping and countable at a glance, and a column holding more than nine of them stands its tokens higher than the column is tall, which is the first thing wrong with it. When ten tokens tie, a drawn band wraps them, they become one token of the next kind, and that one token walks left along a carry lane 12 tall that runs under the circle band, at one slow breath per column, and settles in the circle above the column to the left, where its digit is written in vermilion. Slow trade runs that whole movement at walking pace and can be run again on any column without the sum being touched. A column that still has an uncounted digit in the circle above it will not close: its outline thickens, it does not dim, and the circle holds amber until everything standing in the column, the circle included, has been counted out one token at a time. A carried digit dropped in any circle but its own is handed straight back with the column it belongs to lit and its heading read. No circle is ever drawn above the ones column, because there is no column to its right for anything to come from. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a column total, a carried digit or a whole sum is asked for, and on the first phase a word pad of the mat's place names, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands and lakhs, so that a trade can be said in both its halves with two presses. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number being added is deep blue, the answer standing under the rule is green, a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, a rounded number is rose, the digit under discussion or the one that is missing is amber, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows the sum with the most trades in it, every circle still filled, and the tally of how many columns carried.

phases.win: ten tokens tie into one and walk left, leaving six behind
phases.does: runs the slow trade and reads off what the sixteen hundreds became
phases.goal: ten of any place trade for one of the place to its left
phases.says: Ten of these make one of those. Say the trade out loud.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many hundreds make one thousand, and how many thousands make one ten thousand?
phases.feels: ten things you can count go in and one thing comes out, and nothing was lost on the way
phases.hands: Bundle loose straws into tens with rubber bands, then bundle ten of those bundles into a hundred. Make them say each trade in the page's own words before a single thing is written down: ten hundreds are one thousand, seventeen hundreds are one thousand and seven hundreds.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many tokens are standing in the column? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them does it take to tie one of the next kind? Third rung: ten single tokens only are put in the ones column and the child runs the trade on those. The word pad of place names stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the total is correct and the column is where it was counted, so that is where it looks as though it goes.
wrong.move: writes the whole count in the hundreds column, because that is what the column holds.
wrong.screen: the column is drawn with its one square and all of its tokens standing in it, so the tokens stand higher than the column is tall; then ten of them tie into one thousand token at walking pace and walk left up the lane, six are left standing behind them, and the column can close. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: the trade is spoken as ten hundreds make one thousand, and it is easy to hear the ten and the thousand and lose the one.
wrong.move: trades ten hundreds for ten thousands, keeping the ten and changing only the name.
wrong.screen: the ten hundred tokens go into the tie and exactly one thousand token comes out of it, and both are held on the stage together, the ten counted aloud on one side and the single token on the other; the tray's thousand token is then laid beside the ten hundred tokens in a row, so the two can be measured against each other.

phases.screen: a hundreds column holding sixteen tokens, with the thousands column empty
phases.soWhat: Ten of any place trade for one of the place on its left, and that trade is regrouping.
phases.concept: Ten of one place make one of the next

phases.win: the column closes holding a single digit and the circle above the next one fills
phases.does: writes the digit that stays and sends the rest to the circle above the next column
phases.goal: the right hand digit stays and the rest leaves the column
phases.says: Only one digit fits in a column. What has to leave?
phases.check: A tens column comes to fifteen. Which digit stays in the column, and where does the other one go?
phases.feels: the total will not fit in the square, and only one digit of it is allowed to stay
phases.hands: Write a column sum on squared paper, one digit to a square, where the ones column comes to more than nine. Ask the child to fit that total into the one square the ones column has, and let them try it before anything is said.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many squares does a column have? Second rung, the phase's: which digit of the total stays in it? Third rung: a single column is left on the mat with a total past nine standing in tokens, and the child says what stays and what leaves. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: both digits of the total are true, so writing both of them looks like telling the whole truth.
wrong.move: writes the whole two digit total under the ones column, using two squares for it.
wrong.screen: what the child wrote stays under the rule, and the mat rules the ones column back to its own single square, so the second digit is left standing outside the column it was written in; the heading above that stray digit lights, and the column's tokens are then counted into a tie of ten with the rest left over.

wrong.why: the square is filled and the column looks finished, and the part that would not fit looks like something left over rather than something that has to go somewhere.
wrong.move: writes the right hand digit and lets the rest go, because the right hand digit is what fits.
wrong.screen: the token that was dropped is drawn back onto the stage, standing alone in the lane above the next column, and the sum is read out twice, once with it and once without; the two totals stand one under the other and what lies between them is exactly the token that was let go.

phases.screen: a ones column that has come to fourteen with one square to write in
phases.soWhat: A column keeps its right hand digit and the rest goes into the circle above the next column.
phases.concept: A column can only keep one digit

phases.win: the column will not close until the circle has been counted, and then it does
phases.does: counts the circle in with the column before closing it
phases.goal: the carry is added in with that column, not after it
phases.says: You carried one. Put it in the next column before you add, not after.
phases.check: You carried one into the hundreds column. When does it get added in, and why never at the end?
phases.feels: the little digit above the column is not a note, it is one of the things you are adding
phases.hands: Work a sum on paper that trades twice, and put a finger on each carried digit as the column it belongs to is added. Make them say the whole column out loud with the carried digit named first, before the digits that were printed.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is standing in the circle above this column? Second rung, the phase's: has it been counted in yet? Third rung: one column is left on the mat with two digits under it and a filled circle above it, and the child counts the three of them. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a small digit sitting above the mat looks like a note to remember rather than a number standing in the column.
wrong.move: adds the column, writes its digit, and then adds the carried one on at the end of the whole sum.
wrong.screen: the column will not close: its outline thickens and does not dim, the circle above it holds amber, and everything standing in the column is counted out one token at a time with the circle counted in among them. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: the digit came out of that column, so the circle nearest to it looks like the place it belongs.
wrong.move: drops the carried digit into the circle above the column it came out of.
wrong.screen: the digit is handed straight back and the column it belongs to is lit one place to the left with its heading read out; the circle it was dropped into is left visibly empty, and the lane between the two columns is drawn so that the way the token travelled can be followed with a finger.

phases.screen: a tens column with two digits below and a filled circle above
phases.soWhat: The carried digit is added in with its own column, before that column is closed.
phases.concept: The carried digit joins the next column

phases.win: a circle fills with a two and the sum still closes correctly
phases.does: works the sum through and reads what each circle is holding
phases.goal: nothing changes with three addends except how big the carry can be
phases.says: Three numbers now. Can the carry be bigger than one?
phases.check: Three digits in one column come to twenty four. What is written in the column, and what is carried?
phases.feels: three numbers in one column, and the circle above it takes a two
phases.hands: Put three four digit numbers on paper, one under the other, and add the ones column out loud before anybody writes anything. Ask how big that column could get, and hear the guesses, before you let them find out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what did this column come to? Second rung, the phase's: how many tens are inside that total? Third rung: one column is left on the mat with three digits under it and the child ties its tokens with slow trade on. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every carry in every sum so far has been a single one, so the circle looks like a place that only ever takes a one.
wrong.move: carries one out of a column that came to more than nineteen, because a carry has always been one.
wrong.screen: the column is emptied back into tokens and tied slowly: ten tie and walk left, then the tokens still standing are counted and ten of those tie and walk left too, so two tokens arrive in the same circle and the circle writes a two. The child's digit stays in the answer slot beside it.

wrong.why: two numbers at a time is what every sum so far has had, so three numbers look like two sums stacked up.
wrong.move: adds the first two strips, writes their total under the rule, and then adds the third to that in a second sum.
wrong.screen: both ways are worked on the same mat, the three strips in one column sum on the left of the working area and the two step working on the right, and the two totals stand side by side and agree; the number of columns that had to be counted is written under each of them.

phases.screen: the mat with three strips on it and a ones column past nineteen
phases.soWhat: Three addends change how big the carried digit can be and nothing else at all.
phases.concept: Three addends carry in the same way

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the tens column of the three addend sum is closed. Its tokens gather and ten of them tie into a single hundred and walk left up the lane. The tokens still standing are counted, and there are more than ten of them left, so ten of those tie as well and a second hundred follows the first into the same circle. The circle writes a two in vermilion, and a child who has watched every carry so far be a one sees a carry that is not. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the hundreds column of the mat stands full of tokens, more of them than the column is tall, with the thousands column beside it ruled and empty and the tray below holding the four kinds of token. On the second a ones column has already been counted past nine and the single square under the rule waits. On the third a tens column stands with two digits below it and the circle above it already filled. On the fourth three strips lie on the mat and the ones column of them has been counted past nineteen. The running count at the top left holds the columns that have traded against the columns closed so far, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the tenth token in the full column, or the square under the rule, or the filled circle, or the third strip, gives one slow pulse while the voice says that a column holding more than nine will not close. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Two addends or three, any numbers up to six digits, with the slow trade, the carry count and the replay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on trading ten for one, writing the carry where it belongs and adding it into its column.
voiceLines: A column that holds more than nine will not close. Watch what leaves it.
Ten of these make one of those. Say the trade out loud.
Only one digit fits in a column. What has to leave?
You carried one. Put it in the next column before you add, not after.
Three numbers now. Can the carry be bigger than one?
Another sum. Watch for the column that will not close.
Free play. Two numbers or three, slow trade on or off, tokens whenever you want them.
Empty it back into tokens and tie them again, slowly.
Every column kept one digit, and every trade landed in the circle it belonged in.

observations.why: Ten of any place is exactly one of the place on its left.
observations.soWhat: Nothing is gained or lost in a trade; the same amount is standing in fewer tokens.
observations.observe: Ten tokens went into the tie and one token came out of it.

observations.why: A column has one square, and the rest of the total is worth a whole place more.
observations.soWhat: What is written is what was left, and what is carried is what would not fit.
observations.observe: The column closed holding one digit, and it was the right hand digit of the total.

observations.why: The carried digit is one of the things standing in that column.
observations.soWhat: A carry is added in with its column, never added on at the end of the sum.
observations.observe: The next column would not close while the circle above it still held an uncounted digit.

observations.why: Three digits and a carry coming in can take a column past nineteen.
observations.soWhat: The carried digit is whatever will not fit, and that is not always one.
observations.observe: With three addends a circle filled with a two.

observations.why: A traded token is worth one of the place it moved into, and nothing lies to the right of the ones.
observations.soWhat: Nothing is ever carried into the ones column, which is why that column can always be added first.
observations.observe: Every carried token settled above the column to the left of the one it came out of, and no circle was ever drawn above the ones.

source_tool.description: The same column mat, now with a tray of loose tokens beside it and a small circle drawn above every column. A column that comes to more than nine will not close: its tokens gather, ten of them tie into a single token of the next place up, and that one token walks left into the circle above the next column, where it waits. The waiting token cannot be ignored, because the next column will not close until everything in it has been counted, the circle included. A slow trade control runs the bundling at walking pace so the ten going in and the one coming out can both be watched. A carried digit dropped anywhere other than its own circle is handed back with the column it belongs to lit. The mat takes two addends or three, and with three the column totals climb far enough that a circle can hold a two, which is the thing a child who has only ever carried a one does not expect. A carry count along the top keeps a tally of how many columns had to trade.
source_tool.art_direction: A token tray beside a carry mat / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that tie themselves together, a rule under the last addend, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A sum is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the addends stacked with their right ends aligned, and a horizontal rule between the last addend and the sum. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach adding.
A carried digit is always drawn small, above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, and a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, so an estimate is told apart from an exact answer before either is read. The digit under discussion, which is usually the one that is missing, is amber. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carry is told apart by being small and sitting above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Empty it back into tokens and tie them again, slowly.
voice.onNext: Another sum. Watch for the column that will not close.
voice.opening: A column that holds more than nine will not close. Watch what leaves it.
voice.onFinish: Every column kept one digit, and every trade landed in the circle it belonged in.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Two numbers or three, slow trade on or off, tokens whenever you want them.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Ten of one place make one of the next
A column can only keep one digit
The carried digit joins the next column
Three addends carry in the same way

placement.where: After the four trades have been said out loud from the page and before the first regrouping sum is attempted on paper. The tool is what makes the ten going in and the one coming out one event rather than two.

answer_key.rule: Ten of any place make one of the next place up, so a column that comes to more than nine is split: the right hand digit stays in the column and the rest is carried into the circle above the next column on the left. The carried digit is added in with everything else in that column, not added on at the end. With three addends a column can come to more than nineteen, so the carried digit can be larger than one.
answer_key.wrong: The column is emptied back into tokens and bundled again slowly, with the ten going in and the one coming out drawn as one move. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Ten hundreds make one thousand, so ten of the sixteen tie into a single thousand.
That leaves six hundreds behind in the column.
So 16 hundreds is 1 thousand and 6 hundreds.
items.question: A hundreds column comes to 16 hundreds. Write that as thousands and hundreds.
items.checkpoint: Ten of any place trade for one of the place to its left.
items.misconception: Writing 16 in the hundreds column, which no single column can hold.

steps: The ones column is 6 + 8 = 14, which is 1 ten and 4 ones, so 4 stays and 1 is carried.
The tens column is 7 + 5 with the carried 1, which is 13, so 3 stays and 1 is carried.
Working on left gives 6 in the hundreds, 2 with a carry in the thousands and 6 in the ten thousands, which is 62,634.
items.answer: The ones column comes to 14, so 4 is written and 1 ten is carried, and the sum is 62,634
items.question: Add 38,476 and 24,158, and say what happens in the ones column.
items.checkpoint: A column that comes to more than nine keeps only its right hand digit.
items.misconception: Writing 14 under the ones column and carrying nothing.

steps: The ones column is 9 + 7 = 16, so 6 stays and 1 goes into the circle above the tens.
The tens column is 8 + 4 and the carried 1, which is 13, so 3 stays and 1 goes above the hundreds.
Working the rest the same way gives 9 hundreds, 2 thousands with a carry, and 8 ten thousands, which is 82,936.
items.answer: 82,936, with each carried digit added into the next column along with its own digits
items.question: Add 47,689 and 35,247, and say where each carried digit is added.
items.checkpoint: The carried digit is added in with the column it sits above.
items.misconception: Adding the carried ones on at the end of the whole sum instead of into the next column.

steps: The ones column is 8 + 6 + 5 = 19, so 9 stays and 1 is carried.
The tens column is 7 + 5 + 9 and the carried 1, which is 22, so 2 stays and 2 are carried.
The hundreds come to 16 with that carry, the thousands to 9 and the ten thousands to 6, which gives 69,629.
items.answer: 69,629, and the tens column carries 2 rather than 1
items.question: Add 23,478; 14,256; and 31,895.
items.checkpoint: With three addends a column can pass nineteen, so the carry can be more than one.
items.misconception: Carrying only 1 out of the tens column, because a carry is assumed always to be one.

items.question: Add 62,958 and 19,647, and say how many columns had to carry.
Four goods routes measure 1,428 km, 2,065 km, 1,739 km and 2,214 km. What is their total length?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: fills a column with the loose tokens its digits stand for
ties ten tokens into one of the next place up at walking pace
takes the carried digit and holds it above the next column
refuses to close a column until the circle above it has been counted in
adds a third strip to the mat, so a column can carry more than one
tallies how many columns had to trade in this sum
walks the finished sum again showing only the trades

teaching_notes: Say the four trades out loud from the page before the tool is opened, and get them said the long way every time: ten hundreds are one thousand, seventeen hundreds are one thousand and seven hundreds. Then use slow trade for the first few columns, because at full speed the bundle is invisible and what is learnt is a mark rather than a move. The close column control is the whole tool: a column that will not close until the circle above it has been counted in is the difference between a carry that is written down and a carry that is used. When the third strip goes on, stop and ask before anybody works it out whether the circle can hold more than one. The answer surprises them and it should. Come back to the opening railway table here, because the total length of the routes is exactly this: a column sum of seven numbers with trades in most columns, and it is the first point in the chapter at which the opening question can honestly be answered.
generation_prompt: Build a regrouping tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A ruled column mat with a named heading over each column and a small empty circle drawn above every column, taking two addend strips or three. A token tray fills any column with the loose tokens its digits stand for. When a column passes nine, ten of its tokens visibly tie into a single token of the next place up and that token walks left into the circle above the next column, with a slow trade control that runs the whole bundling at walking pace. The close column control refuses to close a column while the circle above it still holds an uncounted digit, and lights that circle when refused. A carried digit dragged to any circle other than its own is handed back with its proper column lit. With three strips on the mat a column total can pass nineteen and the circle takes a two. A carry count along the top tallies how many columns traded, and a replay control walks the finished sum again showing only the trades. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fill a column and watch what happens when it passes nine. Ten tokens tie into one and walk left into the circle. Write the digit that stays, then count the circle in when you work the next column. Try it with three numbers and see how big the carry can get.
